title: Hands in prayer
hook: folded on the chest, below the navel, or at the sides, depending on school

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Amman Message, and your line: eight schools, one ummah. Which of those eight names still feels like a stranger to you? Day one thousand two hundred seven.

Stand at the back of a big mosque during prayer and watch the hands. A row of shoulders, all facing one way, and then the hands. One man has his right hand over his left, low, just under the navel. The man beside him holds his higher, near the chest. Two places down, someone's arms hang straight at his sides. Nobody turns to correct anybody. They bow together, go down together, rise together. Same prayer, same imam, three different pairs of hands. Each of them learned it from somewhere. Today, why.
screen: `WATCH THE HANDS.` → `LOW, HIGH, AT THE SIDES.` → `NOBODY CORRECTS ANYBODY.`

segments.voice: First, a report the schools share. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahl ibn Sa'd says people were told to place the right hand on the left forearm in prayer. Holding, called qabd, has a text behind it. Next, the question that text leaves: where? The report says right over left. It doesn't say how high. So the schools weighed other reports, and different answers came out. Hanafi scholars teach men to hold the hands below the navel. Shafi'i scholars place them below the chest and above the navel. In the Hanbali school, below the navel is a well-known view, with room for other places. And some readers point to reports placing the hands on the chest itself. Then, the arms at the sides. That's called sadl, letting the hands hang. In the Maliki school, a report from Imam Malik is read as disliking holding in the obligatory prayers, and in Maliki mosques you may see arms down. The Ja'fari school teaches the arms at the sides, hands resting on the thighs, and so do the Zaydis and the Ibadis. Last, why it matters on an ordinary day. Each of these is a reading of reports from the same Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, passed down by different teachers. In the same row, the man with low hands and the man with hanging arms are each praying as their own school teaches. A stranger's hands aren't a mistake. They're a map of who taught him.
screen: `SAHL: RIGHT HAND OVER LEFT.` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY HOW HIGH.` · `SADL: THE ARMS AT THE SIDES.` · `HANDS ARE A MAP OF TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray as your school teaches, or simply notice your hands. If you pray, stand for a moment and place your hands where you learned to, and ask yourself who taught you. A parent, an imam, a video, a friend. If you don't pray, let your hands rest wherever they fall: in your lap, on your knees, at your sides. Feel the weight of them. Then think of someone who taught you to do something with your hands, tie a knot, hold a pen, knead dough. Stay with that person for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Hands in prayer. Held below the navel, below the chest, on the chest, or at the sides, depending on school; each passed down by a teacher. Today's word.

Your line: different hands. Today, when you see someone do a familiar thing in an unfamiliar way, ask who taught them before you decide it's wrong. Tomorrow, one word, aloud or under the breath. Day one thousand two hundred seven.

howItsDone: In the standing of prayer, Hanafis hold the right hand over the left below the navel, Shafi'is below the chest, Hanbalis below the navel or as their school allows; Malikis following Malik's reported view, and Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi Muslims, pray with their arms at their sides.

pairs: below the chest, above the navel

myth: praying with the arms at the sides is a modern innovation
it is the teaching of the Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi schools, and of Malikis reading a report from Imam Malik.
Sahl ibn Sa'd's report says the right hand goes over the left
it does, in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it doesn't say how high.
every Sunni school puts the hands in the same place
Hanafi below the navel, Shafi'i below the chest, and the Hanbali school allows more than one place.

fork.setup: you're praying in a crowded row. the man beside you lets his arms hang at his sides. what do you do?
options: keep praying; his hands follow his school.
fork.reveal: letting the arms hang is the teaching of Malikis and of the Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi schools. he is praying as his school teaches.

original.note: Arabic: letting hang; in prayer, standing with the arms at the sides. its partner word is qabd, holding.

trapdoor: what you thought: there's one right place for the hands, and everyone else is wrong.
what it means: the shared report says right over left; how high, or whether to hold at all, depends on the school's reading.
what a scholar hears: Sahl ibn Sa'd in al-Bukhari, the Maliki debate over Malik's report, and qabd against sadl.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 740 (Sahl ibn Sa'd: right hand on the left forearm)

notes: Editor: removed the claim that the Amman Message counts anyone's prayer valid (it names schools as Muslim; it does not rule on prayer), in the teach and the fork reveal; 'a careful reading of the same Prophet' fixed; word segment no longer repeats the 'careful reading' line.
Bukhari 740: confirm number and paraphrase ('people were commanded to place the right hand on the left forearm').

School positions (Hanafi men below the navel; Shafi'i below the chest above the navel; Hanbali below the navel as a well-known view, with latitude; some readers on the chest): confirm. Women's position in the Hanafi school (on the chest) deliberately not covered.
Maliki sadl tied to a report from Malik (al-Mudawwana) read as disliking qabd in obligatory prayer; 'often' in North and West Africa: confirm framing and soften if needed.
Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi practice of sadl: confirm; Ja'fari hands resting on the thighs.
howItsDone uses 'usually' and 'many Malikis': confirm or soften.
